# Motivation: functional data in large epidemiological studies



## National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES)

![](figs/nhanes.png)

::: {.notes}
Large, nationally representative survey of over 15,000 ppts every two years
2011-2014: collected high freq accel data from 7 days, in addition to health, nutrition, etc.
:::

::: {.notes}

We're statisticians - we want to quantify this difference - we need to fit a model! 

::: 


## Function on scalar regression (FoSR)

<div style="font-size: 115%;">


Model: $$\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{PA}_i(s)] = \beta_0(s) + \beta_1(s)\mathbb{I}\{\mathrm{sex}_i=\mathrm{male}\} + \sum_{k=2}^{7}\beta_k(s)\mathbb{I}\{\mathrm{agecat}_i=k\} $$ 

$i$: participant; 

$s \in \{1, \dots, 1440\}$: each minute of the day


</div>

::: {.notes}
Outcome: steps profile over the course of the day (function) 

Predictors: age, sex (scalars)

Interpretation
  $\beta_0(s)$: expected steps for reference sex category and reference age category
   Can be interpreted at specific points of the day (e.g., how many more steps do males take at 12pm, holding age constant

:::

## FoSR: model fitting 

::: {.incremental}

<div style="font-size: 150%;">
+ Fast univariate inference (FUI) [@Cui2021]

+ Fit separate (univariate) GLM at each point $s$, smooth the resulting point estimates 

+ Bootstrap to get confidence bands 

+ Other methods for FoSR exist: benefits of FUI in this application will become clear shortly 

</div>

:::

::: {.notes}

Could also fit with penalized splines

:::

# 

![](figs/Traffic-Signal-Stop-Sign-PNG.png)

## NHANES is not a random sample! 


![](figs/nhanes_sample.gif)

Individuals sampled in geographic clusters, minority groups oversampled 

Are estimates from FoSR valid for population-level inference? 


<div style=" position: absolute; bottom: -1em; left: 10em; font-size: 0.6em; color: #777; "> [NHANES Sample Design Tutorial](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/tutorials/sampledesign.aspx) </div>

::: {.notes}

What happens if we ignore? 

::: 

## NHANES is not a random sample! 

<div style="font-size: 135%;">

::: {.incremental}

+ Ignoring the sampling structure can lead to: 

  + Biased **estimation** (need to account for weights to make survey look like population) 
  + Incorrect **inference** (individuals in same stratum/PSU have correlated data; failure to account can under/overestimate variance) 


+ **No** method exists for function on scalar regression under complex surveys


::: 
</div>

## Survey terminology 

<div style="font-size: 135%;">

::: {.incremental}

+ Survey weight: number of people in the population represented by the sampled person
  + $\text{weight} \propto \frac{1}{\text{probability of selection}}$
  + In complex surveys like NHANES, weights also account for complex, multistage design, nonresponse, and post-stratification to match US population^[https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/tutorials/Weighting.aspx]
  
+ Stratum: larger geographic location 

+ Cluster or Primary Sampling Unit (PSU): smaller area within stratum, such as zip code or city block 


::: 

</div>

# Proposed solution: let's combine some existing methods 

## Survey function on scalar regression 

<div style="font-size: 135%;">


::: {.incremental}



+ GLMs: methods and software exist to take into account weights (estimation) and correlation between clusters for inference ($\texttt{svyglm}$, $\texttt{svycoxph}$) [@surveys] 

+ FUI is built on separate GLMs

+ **Idea**: incorporate survey weights into the GLMs (estimation) and use survey-aware replication/bootstrap methods for inference 

:::

</div>

# Implementation

## Fit survey-weighted GLM at each point along the functional domain 



```{r mimsex1}
#| cache: true 


mims_small |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("min")) |>
```

## What about inference? 

<div style="font-size: 135%;">

::: {.incremental}

+ Standard errors from weighted GLMs don't account for correlation between individuals in same stratum/PSU 
+ Survey-aware replication methods generate $B$ sets of survey weights (analogous to bootstrap replicates), accounting for strata/PSU structure
+ Fit a model on each replicate and estimate standard errors from set of replicates 
+ Several methods exist, we focus on balanced repeated replication (BRR) [@BRR]

:::

</div>


## Inference: BRR 

Choose one PSU from each stratum, double weights for each individual in selected PSU, fit model 

```{r brr vis}
#| cache: true 

sample_structure = tibble(
  sample_type = rep(c("Full Sample", "Replicate 1", "Replicate 2", "Replicate 3", "Replicate 4", "Replicate B"), each = 4),
  stratum = rep(1:4, 6),
  unit1 = rep(TRUE, 24),
  unit2 = rep(TRUE, 24)) |> 
  mutate(
    unit1 = case_when(
      sample_type == "Replicate 1" ~ FALSE,
      sample_type == "Replicate 2" ~ stratum %in% c(2, 4),
      sample_type == "Replicate 3" ~ stratum %in% c(3, 4),
      sample_type == "Replicate 4" ~ stratum %in% c(2, 3),
      sample_type == "Full Sample" ~ TRUE,
      sample_type == "Replicate B" ~ TRUE
    ),
    unit2 = case_when(
      sample_type == "Replicate 1" ~ TRUE,
      sample_type == "Replicate 2" ~ stratum %in% c(1, 3),
      sample_type == "Replicate 3" ~ stratum %in% c(1, 2),
      sample_type == "Replicate 4" ~ stratum %in% c(1, 4),
      sample_type == "Full Sample" ~ TRUE,
      sample_type == "Replicate B" ~ FALSE
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("unit"), names_to = "unit", values_to = "included")

ggplot(sample_structure %>% filter(included), 
       aes(x = unit, y = factor(stratum), fill = unit)) +
  geom_tile(color = "#f6f5f3", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~sample_type, ncol = 6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("unit1" = "#65CCFFFF", "unit2" = "#FFCC65FF"),
                    labels = c("Unit 1", "Unit 2")) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("1", "2")) +
  labs(title = "Balanced Repeated Replication Schematic",
       y = "Stratum", x = "Cluster", fill = "Cluster") +
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
        panel.grid = element_blank(), 
        panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

```

## Inference: BRR 

From $B$ BRR replicates, get pointwise variance

```{r show pw variance}
#| cache: true 

boot_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = s, y = value, group = name)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "tp", k = 21), se = FALSE, alpha = 0.2, linewidth = .1, color = "slategrey") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1440, 240),
                     labels = c("00:00", "04:00", "08:00", "12:00", "16:00", "20:00", "24:00")) +
  labs(x = "Time of Day", y = "Difference in MIMS: Males minus Females",
       title = "Coefficient function replicates") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  geom_smooth(data = mdf, inherit.aes = FALSE, aes(x = s, y = value),
              method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "tp", k = 21), se = FALSE, 
              color = "black") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Original estimate" = "dashed"), name = "") +
  geom_point(data = smoothed_points, aes(x = s, y = smoothed), 
             inherit.aes = FALSE, size = .5) +
  annotate(geom = "label", color = "#FF2A00FF",
           label = "Estimate variance of coefficient from point estimates\nat each point along the functional domain",
           x = 60, y = -1, hjust = 0) +
  annotate(geom = "curve", 
           x = 60, xend = 1,           
           y = -.9, yend = median(smoothed_points$smoothed),  
           curvature = 0.3,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), type = "closed"),
           color = "#FF2A00FF",
           linewidth = 0.7) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-2, 1.1))

```

## Inference: BRR 

Use pointwise variance to get pointwise confidence intervals

```{r ci vis}
#| cache: true 


male_vec = unname(male_vec)
fit = gam(male_vec ~ s(seq_along(male_vec), bs = "tp", k = 20), method = "GCV.Cp")

male_smooth = fitted(fit)

male_smooth |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  mutate(s = row_number(),
         var = var_smooth,
         lower = value - 1.96 * sqrt(var_smooth),
         upper = value + 1.96 * sqrt(var_smooth)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = s, y = value, color = var)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, x = s), alpha = .5) +
  geom_point(size = .3, alpha = .5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1440, 240),
                     labels = c("00:00", "04:00", "08:00", "12:00", "16:00", "20:00", "24:00")) +
  labs(x = "Time of Day", y = "Difference in MIMS: Males minus Females",
       title = "Estimated coefficient and pointwise 95% confidence intervals") +
  scale_color_paletteer_c("ggthemes::Red-Gold", name = "Pointwise Variance", limits = c(0, 0.03)) +
  theme_sub_legend(position = c(0, 0),
                   justification = c(0, 0),
                   box.background = element_rect(fill = "#f6f5f3", color = NA)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-2, 1.1)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), linetype = "dashed", color = "slategrey") 

  
```

## Joint inference 

<div style="font-size: 135%;">

::: {.incremental}

+ Pointwise intervals ask "are females more active than males at 8AM?"
  + $\beta(s) \neq 0$ at $s$?

+ Might also want to ask whether the entire daily activity pattern is different between males and females
  + Joint significance: $\beta(s) \neq 0 \text{ } \forall s$?

+ We have a multiplicity problem if we use the pointwise intervals: we're testing $\beta(s) = 0$ $1440$ times 
  + Expect $1440 \cdot 0.05 = 72$ false positives under the null

::: 

</div>

## Joint inference: Bonferroni correction 

Bonferroni: $\alpha = \frac{0.05}{1440}; z_{1-\alpha/2}=3.98$


```{r bonferroni}
#| cache: true 
q = qnorm(1-3.472222e-05)
# bonferroni correction 
male_smooth |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  mutate(s = row_number(),
         var = var_smooth,
         lower = value - 1.96 * sqrt(var_smooth),
         lower2 = value - q * sqrt(var_smooth),
         upper = value + 1.96 * sqrt(var_smooth),
         upper2 = value + q * sqrt(var_smooth)) |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = s, ymin = lower2, ymax = upper2, fill = "Bonferroni adjusted"), color = NA) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = s, ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = "Pointwise"), color = NA) +
  geom_smooth(data = mdf, inherit.aes = FALSE, aes(x = s, y = value),
              method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "tp", k = 21), se = FALSE, 
              color = "black") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1440, 240),
                     labels = c("00:00", "04:00", "08:00", "12:00", "16:00", "20:00", "24:00")) +
  labs(x = "Time of Day", y = "Difference in MIMS: Males minus Females",
       title = "Estimated coefficient and 95% confidence intervals") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey", "#0072B2FF"), name = "") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), linetype = "dashed", color = "slategrey") +
  theme_sub_legend(position = c(0, 0),
                   justification = c(0, 0),
                   box.background = element_rect(fill = "#f6f5f3", color = NA)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-2, 1.1))

```

## Joint inference: Bonferroni correction


<div style="font-size: 135%;">

::: {.incremental}
+ Bonferroni gives valid joint coverage, but it is conservative because tests are not independent
  + $\hat{\beta}(8:00\text{am})$ and $\hat{\beta}(8:01\text{am})$ are highly correlated 
+ How can we adjust our CIs to take into account correlation $and$ multiplicity (CMA)? [@fda_book]


:::


</div> 

## Joint inference: intuition

<div style="font-size: 135%;">

::: {.incremental}

+ The coefficient is jointly significant if the confidence band excludes zero everywhere 
+ Joint significance $\iff$ all standardized coefficient estimates exceed the critical value in abs. value
+ Under the null, how big would the largest $|z|$ get? 
+ Want to find critical value $q$ that largest $|z|$ exceeds only $5$\% of the time under the null
+ Depends on the correlation of our coefficients  
:::

</div>

## Joint inference: CMA 
 
**Step 1**: recognize that coefficient estimates are multivariate Normal 
$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \big(\hat{\beta}(s_1), \hat{\beta}(s_2), \dots, \hat{\beta}(s_L)\big)^T \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}, \mathbf{V}_\beta)$$

## Joint inference: CMA 
 
**Step 1**: recognize that coefficient estimates are multivariate Normal 
$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \big(\hat{\beta}(s_1), \hat{\beta}(s_2), \dots, \hat{\beta}(s_L)\big)^T \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}, \mathbf{V}_\beta)$$

**Step 2**: Standardize to get z-scores

$$\mathbf{Z} = \frac{(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} - \boldsymbol{\beta})}{\mathbf{D}_\beta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{C}_\beta)$$
where $\mathbf{D}_\beta = \sqrt{\text{diag}(\mathbf{V}_\beta)}$ and $\mathbf{C}_\beta$ is the correlation matrix, in practice estimated via BRR replicates 


::: {.notes} 
This cov matrix $\mathbf{V}_\beta$ is what we need to find out CMA critical value 
+ Diagonal entries: uncertainty at each time point 
+ Off-diagonal entries: correlation across time points 
:::

## Joint inference: CMA 
 
**Step 1**: recognize that coefficient estimates are multivariate Normal 
$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \big(\hat{\beta}(s_1), \hat{\beta}(s_2), \dots, \hat{\beta}(s_L)\big)^T \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}, \mathbf{V}_\beta)$$

**Step 2**: Standardize to get z-scores

$$\mathbf{Z} = \frac{(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} - \boldsymbol{\beta})}{\mathbf{D}_\beta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{C}_\beta)$$
where $\mathbf{D}_\beta = \sqrt{\text{diag}(\mathbf{V}_\beta)}$ and $\mathbf{C}_\beta$ is the correlation matrix, in practice estimated via BRR replicates 

**Step 3**: find critical value $q(\mathbf{C}_\beta, 1-\alpha)$ such that

$$P\big(\max_s|Z_s|\leq q\big) = 1-\alpha  \text{, where } \mathbf{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{C}_\beta)$$

::: {.notes}
Use the multivariate normal structure of our estimates. The correlation matrix from BRR tells us how the z-scores at different time points move together. We simulate from this distribution and find the 95th percentile of the max - that's the critical value. Best of both worlds b/w bonferroni and pointwise. Find q using quantile fn from multivariate Normal distribution, or simulate. 

Other approaches: parameter simulations, nonparametric bootstrap of max abs statistic
::: 

## Joint inference: CMA 

<div style="font-size: 90%;">
Bonferroni critical value = $3.98$; CMA critical value = $3.03$; pointwise critical value = $1.96$
</div> 

```{r cma}
#| cache: true 
qn = model$cis$qn[2]
# bonferroni correction 
male_smooth |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  mutate(s = row_number(),
         var = var_smooth,
         lower = value - 1.96 * sqrt(var_smooth),
         lower3 = value - qn * sqrt(var_smooth),
         upper3 = value + qn * sqrt(var_smooth),
         lower2 = value - q * sqrt(var_smooth),
         upper = value + 1.96 * sqrt(var_smooth),
         upper2 = value + q * sqrt(var_smooth)) |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = s, ymin = lower2, ymax = upper2, fill = "Bonferroni adusted"), color = NA) + geom_ribbon(aes(x = s, ymin = lower3, ymax = upper3, fill = "Correlation and multiplicity adjusted (CMA)"), color = NA) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = s, ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = "Pointwise"), color = NA) +
  geom_smooth(data = mdf, inherit.aes = FALSE, aes(x = s, y = value),
              method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "tp", k = 21), se = FALSE, 
              color = "black") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1440, 240),
                     labels = c("00:00", "04:00", "08:00", "12:00", "16:00", "20:00", "24:00")) +
  labs(x = "Time of Day", y = "Difference in MIMS: Males minus Females",
       title = "Estimated coefficient and 95% confidence intervals") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey", "#56B4E9FF", "#0072B2FF"), name = "") +
  theme_sub_legend(position = c(0, 0),
                   justification = c(0, 0),
                   box.background = element_rect(fill = "#f6f5f3", color = NA)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-2, 1.1)) +
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), linetype = "dashed", color = "slategrey") 


```

# Easy enough to implement -- but how do we know if it works? 


## Compare survey-aware vs. unweighted approach with simulation

::: {.incremental}

+ Generate a superpopulation of individuals who belong to a stratum and cluster 
+ Each individual has functional outcome and covariate^[More details in [Appendix](#sec-appendix)]
+ [Optionally] create correlation in functional outcomes within strata and clusters
+ [Optionally] create heterogeneity in covariate effects by strata/cluster
+ Sample from the superpopulation in each iteration of the simulation
  + [Optionally] allow for informative sampling: probability of being included in sample related to functional outcome 
+ Evaluate coverage and estimation error (integrated squared error; ISE = $\int_s \{\hat{\beta}(s) - \beta(s)\}^2ds$)

:::

## Simulated survey data

## Simulation summary 

<div style="font-size: 120%">

::: {.incremental}
+ Unweighted only achieves adequate coverage/comparable estimation error w/ uniform sampling and no stratum/PSU random effects
+ Our method achieves adequate coverage and lower bias than unweighted methods under informative sampling and/or stratum/PSU effects
+ Results hold for Gaussian, Poisson, and binomial data
+ Empirical simulation resampling NHANES curves validated results 

:::
</div> 

## Assumptions 

<div style="font-size: 120%">

**Survey design** 

+ Survey weights are bounded 
+ Inclusion probabilities are positive and correctly specified 
+ For BRR: two PSUs per stratum

</div> 

## Assumptions 

<div style="font-size: 120%">

**Survey design** 

+ Survey weights are bounded 
+ Inclusion probabilities are positive and correctly specified 
+ For BRR: two PSUs per stratum

**Model**

+ $\beta(s)$ is smooth
+ The mean is correctly specified: $E(Y_i(s)|X_i) = g^{-1}(X_i\beta(s))$
+ Functional outcomes $Y_i(s)$ are independent conditional on covariates and survey design

</div> 

## Asymptotics
<div style="font-size: 120%">

**Consistency**

  + Survey-weighted pointwise estimator $\hat{\beta}(s)$ is consistent for the population parameter $\beta(s)$
  + Smoothed estimator $\tilde{\beta}(s)$ is consistent for $\beta(s)$ provided that smoothing parameter $\lambda$ approaches zero at the appropriate rate
  
</div>

## Asymptotics
<div style="font-size: 120%">

**Consistency**

  + Survey-weighted pointwise estimator $\hat{\beta}(s)$ is consistent for the population parameter $\beta(s)$
  + Smoothed estimator $\tilde{\beta}(s)$ is consistent for $\beta(s)$ provided that smoothing parameter $\lambda$ approaches zero at the appropriate rate
  
**Coverage** 

  + Pointwise CIs achieve nominal rate due to consistency of BRR variance estimators, provided smoothing bias of smaller order than standard error
  + Joint CMA intervals achieve nominal coverage under assumption that $\hat{\beta}(s)$ is multivariate normal across the functional domain 
</div>

```{r compare}
    facet_wrap(. ~ var_name, scales = "free_y") +
    geom_ribbon(aes(x = l, ymin = lower_pw, ymax = upper_pw, fill = model2), alpha = .5) +
    # geom_ribbon(aes(x = l, ymin = lower_joint, ymax = upper_joint, fill = model2), alpha = .3) +
    geom_line(aes(color = model2), linewidth = 1.1)  +

      linetype = "dashed"
    ) +

  scale_color_manual(values = c("#009E73FF", "#CC79A7FF")) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks= seq(0, 1440, 4 * 60), labels = c("00:00", "04:00", "08:00", "12:00", "16:00", "20:00", "24:00")) +
    labs(x = "Time of Day", y = "Coefficient Estimate", fill = "Model Type", color = "Model Type") +
    geom_rect(data = disagree_df %>% filter(!brr_sig),
              aes(x = l, y = -2, height = .5, width = 1), fill = "#009E73FF", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    geom_rect(data = disagree_df %>% filter(brr_sig),
              aes(x = l, y = -2, height = .5, width = 1), fill = "#CC79A7FF", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_text(data = annotation_data,
            aes(x = x_label, y = y_label, label = label, hjust = hjust),
```

</div>
![](figs/logo.png){width=20%}

<div style=" position: absolute; bottom: 2em; right: -4em; font-size: 0.7em; color: #777; "> @svy_package </div>

## Computation 

<div style="font-size: 115%;">

::: {.incremental}

+ NHANES model ($B = 500$, $n = 12500$, $L = 1440$) takes under 4 minutes to run on standard computer 
+ Speedups:
  + If predictors $X$ are same across functional domain, instead of fitting a separate model at each time point, we can create $n\times L$ matrix $Y$ by stacking our outcomes and fit $B = (X'WX)^{-1}X'WY$
  + Use QR decomposition instead of calculating $(X'WX)^{-1}$ directly
  + For GLMs, apply above at each step of IRLS or Newton-Raphson 
  + Parallelize bootstrapping 

::: 

</div>


# Summary, Limitations, Future Directions

## Summary

<div style="font-size: 135%;">

::: {.incremental}

+ Developed a method for function on scalar regression under complex survey designs, motivated by physical activity in NHANES
+ Demonstrated importance of approach in presence of informative sampling, within-PSU/strata covariate effects, and/or within-PSU/strata correlation
+ Computationally efficient software for implementation, support for Gaussian, Poisson, and binomial data 
+ Paper on [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.05487)

::: 

</div> 

## Limitations and Future Directions 

<div style="font-size: 135%;">

::: {.incremental}

+ Multilevel data (e.g. multiple days)
+ Full asymptotic treatment 
+ Smoothing order sensitivity 

::: 

</div>

## Smoothing order

+ Our approach is to fit pointwise models, then smooth coefficients
+ An alternative approach would be to smooth outcomes first, then fit pointwise models to the smoothed data
+ With Gaussian data and same linear smoother, approaches are equivalent
+ Difference is in how the smoothing parameter $\lambda$ is selected
+ When smoothing applied to coefficients, whose pointwise variance is $\sigma^2/n$, GCV selects smaller smoothing parameter as $n$ grows, ensuring the estimator is consistent
+ When smoothing is applied to outcomes, pointwise variance is $\sigma^2$, $O(1)$ bias is introduced that doesn't change with sample size
+ If the smooth applied to the outcomes is calibrated to have the same EDF as the smooth applied to the coefficients, comparable performance can be achieved between the two approaches
+ The next few slides illustrate this phenomenon

## Smoothing order

## Smoothing order 

```{r smooth2}
#| cache: true 

# First, get the bias data and determine scaling
bias_data = edf_fix |>
  filter(n == 1000) |>
  select(s, contains("bias")) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -s) |>
  separate_wider_delim(cols = name, delim = "_", names = c("smooth_order", "xx", "var")) |>
  filter(var == "b1")

# Scaling parameters: map bias range to ~[0, 0.5] so it doesn't overlap too much with coverage
bias_range = range(bias_data$value)
scale_factor = 0.4 / max(abs(bias_range))  # scale to fit in lower part of plot
offset = 0.5  # center the bias around 0.5 on the primary axis

# Coverage data
cover_data = edf_fix |>
  filter(n == 1000) |>
  select(s, contains("cover")) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -s) |>
  separate_wider_delim(cols = name, delim = "_", names = c("smooth_order", "xx", "var")) |>
  filter(var == "b1")

# Plot
p1 = ggplot() +
  # Coverage lines (primary axis)
  geom_line(data = cover_data,
            aes(x = s, y = value, color = smooth_order),
            linewidth = 1) +
  # Bias lines (scaled to primary axis)
  geom_line(data = bias_data,
            aes(x = s, y = value * scale_factor + offset, linetype = smooth_order),
            color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#E69F00FF", "#0072B2FF", "#009E73FF"), name = "Coverage",
                     labels = c("Smooth first", "Smooth second", "Smooth first calibrated EDF")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted"), name = "Bias",
                        labels = c("Smooth first", "Smooth second", "Smooth first calibrated EDF")) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Pointwise coverage",
    limits = c(0, 1),
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ (. - offset) / scale_factor, name = "Bias")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Functional Domain",
       title = bquote("Empirical coverage for" ~ beta[1] ~ "at n = 1000")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, color = "darkgrey", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = offset, color = "grey40", linetype = "dotted", alpha = 0.5) +  # zero line for bias
  annotate(geom = "text", label = "Nominal = 0.95", x = 5, y = 0.95,
           color = "darkgrey", size = 3, vjust = -1) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  theme(title = element_text(family = "sans"))

bias_data = edf_fix |>
  filter(n == 1000) |>
  select(s, contains("bias")) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -s) |>
  separate_wider_delim(cols = name, delim = "_", names = c("smooth_order", "xx", "var")) |>
  filter(var == "b0")

# Scaling parameters: map bias range to ~[0, 0.5] so it doesn't overlap too much with coverage
```
